title: How Computers Actually Work: Hardware, OS & Memory
plainExplanation: A computer is an ultra-fast calculator that processes instructions using binary (0s and 1s). It has a brain (CPU) that does math, short-term memory (RAM) where active programs sit, and long-term storage (SSD/HDD) where files remain when powered off. The Operating System (Windows/Mac/Linux) manages these resources so your software can run.
whyItMatters: Programming is writing step-by-step instructions for the CPU and RAM. If you don't understand how memory stores information, concepts like variables, pointers, and memory leaks will feel like magic.
learningObjectives: Distinguish between CPU processing, RAM (volatile memory), and disk storage (persistent)
Explain what an Operating System does in plain English
Understand what a binary digit (bit) and byte represent
commonMistakes: Thinking saving a file means it is saved in RAM forever
Confusing operating system commands with hardware instructions

assessment.title: Computer Architecture & Operating Systems Mastery Check

questions.prompt: You are writing a Python script and your computer suddenly loses power. What happens to variables that were stored in RAM but never written to disk?
options: They remain in RAM and will be restored when turned on
They are completely lost because RAM is volatile memory
The CPU automatically copies them to the hard drive before dying
They get saved in the operating system cache file permanently
questions.correctAnswer: They are completely lost because RAM is volatile memory
questions.explanation: RAM (Random Access Memory) requires continuous electrical current to retain data. When power cuts out, all active RAM contents are wiped.

questions.prompt: A beginner claims: 'I bought 16 GB of RAM so I have enough space to install 5 large 50 GB games!' What fundamental misunderstanding exists here?
options: None, RAM is where games are installed permanently
Confusing RAM (working workspace) with Secondary Storage / SSD (permanent storage)
Games don't need any RAM to run
16 GB is too much memory for games
questions.correctAnswer: Confusing RAM (working workspace) with Secondary Storage / SSD (permanent storage)
questions.explanation: Secondary storage (SSD/HDD) stores installed applications permanently. RAM is volatile working memory loaded only while the game or program is actively running.

questions.prompt: In your own words (or Hinglish: 'Apne shabdon mein'), explain the difference between CPU and RAM using an analogy like a chef and kitchen counter.
questions.correctAnswer: CPU is the chef who does the work/cooking; RAM is the kitchen counter where currently needed ingredients sit; SSD/Storage is the pantry where food is kept long term.
questions.explanation: A complete answer compares CPU to the active worker/processor and RAM to temporary fast-access workspace.
questions.rubricCriteria: ["Identifies CPU as calculation/execution engine", "Identifies RAM as temporary fast workspace", "Contrast with persistent storage"]

title: Mastering the Command Line (Terminal & Shell)
plainExplanation: The terminal is a text-based interface to control your computer. Instead of clicking icons with a mouse (GUI), you type commands (CLI) to create folders, move files, and launch programs. In engineering, almost all servers, cloud tools, and build pipelines run exclusively in the terminal.
whyItMatters: Every developer, ML researcher, and data engineer uses the command line every single day. Without it, you cannot run scripts, manage version control, or deploy applications.
learningObjectives: Navigate directory trees using cd, pwd, and ls/dir
Create, move, rename, and delete files safely
Understand standard input, output, and exit codes
commonMistakes: Using relative paths when an absolute path is needed, or vice-versa
Accidentally deleting non-empty directories without understanding recursive flags

title: Variables, Data Types & Operators in Python
plainExplanation: A variable is a labeled container in memory where your program stores information to use later (e.g. `age = 21` or `name = 'Maya'`). Python has basic data types: integers (whole numbers), floats (decimals), strings (text), and booleans (True or False).
whyItMatters: Variables are the foundational building block of all software. Without them, programs cannot remember user input, calculate results, or make decisions.
learningObjectives: Declare and assign variables following Python naming conventions
Distinguish between int, float, str, and bool
Perform arithmetic and logical operations (+, -, *, /, //, %, ==, !=, and, or)
commonMistakes: Trying to add a string and an integer directly (e.g. '5' + 5) without type conversion

codingChallenge.title: Currency & Bill Split Calculator
codingChallenge.instructions: Write a function `calculate_split(total_bill: float, num_people: int, tip_percentage: float) -> float` that returns the exact amount each person must pay, rounded to 2 decimal places. If num_people is <= 0, return 0.0.

visibleTests.description: $100 with 10% tip split among 4 people = $27.5 each
$50 with 0% tip split among 2 people = $25.0 each

codingChallenge.solutionHint: Calculate total = total_bill * (1 + tip_percentage / 100), then divide by num_people and use round(val, 2).

questions.explanation: Multiplying a string by an integer in Python repeats the string. '10' * 2 results in '1010'. To do math, you must cast with int(x).

questions.prompt: Identify the bug in this code attempting to check if a user is an adult:
options: The variable age is not defined
Using single '=' (assignment) instead of double '==' (comparison) in the if condition
questions.correctAnswer: Using single '=' (assignment) instead of double '==' (comparison) in the if condition
questions.explanation: In Python, `=` assigns a value. `==` checks for equality.

title: Conditionals, Loops & Control Flow
plainExplanation: Control flow is how a program decides which lines of code to run. Conditionals (if, elif, else) allow programs to make decisions based on rules. Loops (for, while) allow programs to repeat an action dozens or millions of times without writing repetitive code.
whyItMatters: Without control flow, code only runs from top to bottom once. Control flow gives software its intelligence and ability to process large amounts of data automatically.
learningObjectives: Use if/elif/else statements to build multi-branch decision trees
Write for-loops over ranges and sequences
Use while-loops with proper termination conditions to avoid infinite loops
Apply break and continue statements correctly
commonMistakes: Creating infinite while-loops by forgetting to update the loop counter variable
Off-by-one errors with range(start, stop) where stop is exclusive

title: Functions, Scope & Clean Code
plainExplanation: A function is a reusable block of code that takes inputs (arguments), performs calculations, and returns an output. It helps you adhere to the DRY principle: Don't Repeat Yourself. Scope determines where in your code variables can be seen and accessed.
whyItMatters: Professional software is made of thousands of small, well-tested functions working together. Without functions, software becomes an unmaintainable wall of spaghetti code.
learningObjectives: Define functions with positional, default, and keyword arguments
Understand the difference between returning a value and printing it
Explain local vs global variable scope
commonMistakes: Using print() inside a function instead of return, preventing the caller from using the result
Accidentally mutating global variables inside local functions
